rules.when: a tiny or surgical change in a known place: a rename, an obvious one-file or config edit, mechanical cleanup, or a quick factual question about how something already works. If it needs a design decision, touches more than one coherent unit, or requires new tests or non-trivial logic, that is IMPLEMENT instead, not QUICK.
rules.why: Claude practical capacity is about 20 versus GPT's about 5 on this fleet - roughly 4:1, not 20:1 - so the smallest ordinary lane defaults to Claude Haiku rather than spending scarcer GPT headroom on trivial work. Haiku and Luna are genuinely interchangeable same-tier candidates for this bucket (both cheap, both low effort, neither semantically preferred over the other) so FirstMate's quota-array procedure may resolve between them after this rule matches. Escalate to anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 at low or medium, by explicit captain choice, only if the task needs more reasoning than either cheap-tier model comfortably gives - never Astra or Opus for ordinary quick work; Opus 5.5 belongs to substantive work in the neighboring categories and Astra to their most exceptional escalations. QUICK versus IMPLEMENT is a size/decision test, not a keyword match: a rename is QUICK, a rename that also requires touching call sites across a module and deciding a new interface is IMPLEMENT.

rules.when: read-only reconnaissance inside our own repository: finding files, callers, existing patterns, an inventory of something, or where a capability is implemented, with no external research and no code changes. If the question is about an external library, API, framework, or standard rather than our own code, that is RESEARCH instead.
rules.why: Ordinary in-repo recon is cheap, bounded work: Haiku at low effort reads and reports without needing deep synthesis. Luna at low effort is a genuinely interchangeable same-tier peer here too, the same capacity-aware pairing QUICK already uses, so FirstMate's quota-array procedure may resolve between them - never Sol, Astra, or Opus for ordinary exploration; those buy nothing a careful read does not already give here. EXPLORE never leaves this repository's own source; RESEARCH is aimed at documentation, APIs, or code outside it - that is the line between them.

rules.when: the same read-only, in-repository reconnaissance as ordinary EXPLORE above, but the reasoning is materially harder than a lookup - for example an unusually tangled call graph, or untangling behavior across many indirection layers. This is a separate, more specific rule within EXPLORE, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick this rule only when the harder-reasoning condition genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: Sonnet at medium effort is the deliberate escalation once plain reading stops being enough, still well short of RESEARCH's external-synthesis effort or DEEP's reasoning-difficulty bar - this is still in-repository recon, just harder recon.

rules.when: questions that require looking outside our own repository: external documentation, third-party APIs, dependency behavior, framework or protocol semantics, standards, or comparing our approach against upstream/OSS source. If the target is our own code rather than an external system, that is EXPLORE instead; if the deliverable is a judgment on a proposed change rather than an information-gathering pass, that is REVIEW instead. If the research is substantial or decision-heavy - its findings will drive a significant design, dependency, migration, or vendor decision, or it must reconcile several conflicting sources into a recommendation - that is the substantial-RESEARCH rule below instead.
rules.why: Sonnet at medium effort is the honest default for ordinary synthesis of external material. Substantial or decision-heavy research is a separate, more specific rule below, never a quota-resolved peer of this ordinary case.

rules.when: the same external-research work as ordinary RESEARCH above, specifically when it is substantial or decision-heavy: the findings will drive a significant design, dependency, migration, or vendor decision, or the research must reconcile several conflicting or incomplete sources into a recommendation. This is a separate, more specific rule within RESEARCH, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick it whenever that condition applies; if uncertain between this and ordinary RESEARCH for research whose conclusions carry decision weight, prefer Opus 5.5.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at high effort is the Opus-biased route for research whose conclusions carry real decision weight. Ordinary lookups and summaries stay on Sonnet 5 medium above; research that specifically benefits from Pi's own tooling stays on the Sol rule below.

rules.when: the same external-research work as ordinary RESEARCH above, specifically when Pi's own tooling (its research-oriented extensions or browsing) is materially better suited to the research target than a cold OMP session. This is a tooling condition, a separate more specific rule, never a default fallback chosen by quota.
rules.why: Sol on Pi is the deliberate route once Pi's own tooling is the better fit for the research target: it fits Pi's tooling profile for this specific job better than a cold OMP session would, at the same medium effort as the OMP default.

rules.when: bounded review of code, a diff, a proposal, or a completion claim for correctness, maintainability, or regression risk - a small, self-contained change a reviewer can hold in their head - not adversarial challenge, not a structural/architecture decision, and not a deep root-cause investigation. If the deliverable is external information-gathering rather than judgment on our own change, that is RESEARCH instead; if independence from the author is the point, that is TENTH-MAN instead; if the question is about system boundaries or long-term structure, that is ARCHITECTURE instead. If the change under review is substantive - meaningful new behavior, a nontrivial refactor, work spanning multiple components, concurrency or other subtle-regression risk, or real cross-component regression risk - that is the substantive-REVIEW rule below instead; if it is critical or high-consequence - release-critical, auth/security, payments, migrations, data integrity, or otherwise a high blast radius - that is the critical-REVIEW rule below instead.
rules.why: Sonnet 5 at high effort covers a bounded review thoroughly without spending Opus 5.5 on a change a careful Sonnet pass fully covers. REVIEW stays on the same OMP session/harness family as implementation because it is not seeking independence - that is what separates it from TENTH-MAN, which deliberately runs on a different model family from the work it challenges. REVIEW also never owns a structural verdict about boundaries or migrations; that judgment belongs to ARCHITECTURE. Substantive and critical review scope are separate, more specific rules below, never quota-resolved peers of this bounded case.

rules.when: the same REVIEW work above, specifically when the change under review is substantive: meaningful new behavior, a nontrivial refactor, work spanning multiple components, concurrency or other subtle-regression risk, or real cross-component regression risk. This is a separate, more specific rule within REVIEW, not a quota-resolved peer of the bounded case: pick it whenever that condition applies; if uncertain between this and bounded REVIEW, prefer Opus 5.5.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at high effort is the Opus-biased reviewer for substantive and cross-component diffs, where a missed subtle regression costs more than the model difference. Critical or high-consequence changes are the separate xhigh rule below.

rules.when: the same REVIEW work above, specifically for critical or high-consequence changes: release-critical work, authentication/security, payments, migrations, data integrity, or otherwise a high blast radius if the review misses something. This is a separate, more specific rule within REVIEW, not a quota-resolved peer of the bounded or substantive case: pick it only when the stakes genuinely warrant it, not by default.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at xhigh effort is reserved for review where the cost of a missed defect is highest - critical or high-consequence changes. A cross-family second reviewer is a separate, more specific rule below, reached for only when an independent-family second opinion is genuinely warranted in addition to this primary review, never a default.

rules.when: the same critical or high-consequence REVIEW work above, specifically when an independent, cross-family second reviewer is warranted in addition to the Opus 5.5 primary review - the highest-stakes cases where a single reviewer's model family should not be the only check. This is a separate, more specific rule within REVIEW, not a quota-resolved peer of the primary critical case: pick it only when that additional independent-family need genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-sol on Pi is REVIEW's cross-family second reviewer, reached for only when the critical case above genuinely needs an independent, differently-sourced check in addition to the Opus 5.5 primary review, never as a routine substitute for it.

rules.when: structural decisions with real blast radius: a system or module boundary, an API or domain boundary, a data model, a migration shape, or any ambiguous design with long-term consequences. Use role architecture. If the deliverable is approval or risk-flagging of someone else's proposal rather than an independent structural recommendation, that is REVIEW instead; if the trigger is a hard-to-diagnose bug or subtle reasoning problem rather than a forward design decision, that is DEEP instead. If the decision is very difficult - unusually high stakes or unusually deep ambiguity - that is the very-difficult-ARCHITECTURE rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Opus 5.5 at high effort is the default for structural decisions with real blast radius. Consultation here never automatically owns the implementation that follows. Escalate to the very-difficult rule below, not this one, once the decision itself is very difficult rather than merely structural. An independent cross-family challenge of an architecture recommendation is TENTH-MAN's job, never a quota peer here.

rules.when: the same structural-decision ARCHITECTURE work above, specifically when the decision is very difficult: unusually high stakes or unusually deep ambiguity beyond the ordinary structural case. This is a separate, more specific rule within ARCHITECTURE, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: pick it only when that condition genuinely applies, not by default.
rules.why: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5 on OMP at xhigh is the single-candidate route for very difficult architecture - a single candidate, not a quota array, so no other model can be selected ahead of Opus 5.5 here. When an independent cross-family second opinion is genuinely needed, dispatch TENTH-MAN against the recommendation (GPT-6 Sol for Claude-authored work) rather than pairing a peer here. openai-codex/gpt-6-astra remains reserved for the separate ultra-exceptional rule below.

rules.when: the same very difficult ARCHITECTURE work above, specifically on the rare occasion even Opus 5.5 at xhigh above is not enough: the decision is so consequential or so deeply contested that the strongest available independent reasoning is warranted regardless of cost. This is a separate, more specific rule within ARCHITECTURE, not a quota-resolved peer of either case above: pick it only when that ultra-exceptional condition genuinely applies, never by default and never merely because the very-difficult rule already matched.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-astra on Pi at xhigh is reached for only on this narrowest, most consequential tier of architecture decision, once Opus 5.5 at xhigh above is not enough. Astra stays limited to this and this configuration's other genuinely exceptional lanes; it is never a routine architecture default.

rules.when: deliberate adversarial challenge: an independent second opinion, a stress test of a plan's assumptions and failure modes, or scrutiny of a completion claim before an expensive or hard-to-reverse commitment - specifically when the work under review was primarily produced by a Claude/Anthropic model. Use role tenth-man. Never routine; risk-triggered or explicitly requested. If the goal is ordinary correctness/maintainability feedback rather than adversarial challenge, that is REVIEW instead; if the goal is a forward structural recommendation rather than challenging an existing one, that is ARCHITECTURE instead.
rules.why: Model-family diversity is the whole point: when the primary author is a Claude/Anthropic model, the challenger runs on Pi with GPT-6 Sol, a different provider and a different harness from the OMP session that likely produced the work, at the lowest cost that still satisfies family diversity. GPT-6 Astra remains available as a separate, more specific escalation below for the most critical or unresolved cases, never a routine default. TENTH-MAN versus DEEP: DEEP investigates why something is broken; TENTH-MAN challenges whether a plan or a completion claim actually holds, broken or not.

rules.when: the same deliberate adversarial-challenge TENTH-MAN work above, specifically when the primary author is still a Claude/Anthropic model and the Sol challenge above leaves the matter critical or genuinely unresolved - not merely difficult, but a case where the stakes or the ambiguity demand the strongest available cross-family challenger. This is a separate, more specific rule within TENTH-MAN, not a routine default: pick it only after the Sol challenge above has genuinely left the matter unresolved, never as a first choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-astra on Pi is reached for only as the most critical or unresolved escalation once the Sol challenge above is not enough, preserving TENTH-MAN's Claude-primary family-diversity route while keeping Astra an explicit, rarely-selected escalation rather than a routine default.

rules.when: the same deliberate adversarial-challenge TENTH-MAN work above, specifically when the work under review was primarily produced by an Astra or other OpenAI-codex model. This is a separate, more specific rule within TENTH-MAN, chosen by which model produced the work under review, not by quota: never let the same provider both author and adversarially review a piece of work.
rules.why: When the primary author is Astra or another OpenAI-codex model, the challenger switches to OMP with Opus 5.5 at xhigh so the reviewer's model family never matches the author's. This enforces the same independence TENTH-MAN's Claude-primary rule enforces, just from the other direction.

rules.when: small or bounded engineering: a focused feature, a bug fix, normal debugging, a small refactor, or writing/repairing tests, contained in one coherent unit with a blast radius you can hold in your head. This is the main coding lane for bounded code changes. If the change is a one-file mechanical edit or a factual question, that is QUICK instead; if it spans many files or the design is not settled yet, that is IMPLEMENT-LARGE instead; if the change is primarily frontend/browser-visible behavior, that is UI/BROWSER instead. If the change is substantive - meaningful new behavior, a nontrivial refactor, work spanning multiple components, real cross-component regression risk, or delicate logic such as races, state machines, or security-sensitive code - that is the substantive-IMPLEMENT rule below instead.
rules.why: Sonnet 5 at high effort for small, bounded code changes: enough care for a clean, tested change without spending Opus 5.5 on work a careful Sonnet pass fully covers. Only move to a neighboring category when one of its specific triggers actually applies. Substantive implementation is a separate, more specific rule below, never a quota-resolved peer of this bounded case.

rules.when: the same IMPLEMENT work above, specifically when the change is substantive: meaningful new behavior, a nontrivial refactor, work spanning multiple components, real cross-component regression risk, or delicate logic - races and concurrency, state machines, security-sensitive code, or coordinated multi-file changes that must stay consistent. This is a separate, more specific rule within IMPLEMENT, not a quota-resolved peer of the bounded case: pick it whenever that condition applies; if uncertain between this and bounded IMPLEMENT, prefer Opus 5.5.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at high effort is the Opus-biased route for substantive implementation - the same 'materially substantive' standard primary-policy.md section 7 uses to require independent review. Bounded work stays on Sonnet 5 above; broad multi-file execution is IMPLEMENT-LARGE.

rules.when: broad multi-file or long-horizon implementation where the direction is mostly already known - more files than IMPLEMENT, but not an unsettled reasoning problem. If the change is small enough to hold in your head, that is IMPLEMENT instead; if the difficulty is in figuring out what is wrong or what is true rather than in the amount of settled work to do, that is DEEP instead.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at high effort is the default for broad, mostly-settled execution: difficult execution, not difficult reasoning - that is what separates IMPLEMENT-LARGE from DEEP. Reasoning-heavy execution is the separate xhigh rule below.

rules.when: the same broad, mostly-settled IMPLEMENT-LARGE work above, specifically when the execution is reasoning-heavy: a long autonomous run whose many coordinated changes each demand careful judgment - interdependent invariants, intricate data transformations, or consistency that must hold across the whole change - even though the overall direction is settled. This is a separate, more specific rule, not a quota-resolved peer of the ordinary case: do not pick it just because many files are touched, and never pick Astra here; if the hard part is finding what is wrong rather than executing a settled plan, that is DEEP instead.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at xhigh is reserved for large execution where per-step reasoning, not throughput, is the limiting factor; ordinary broad execution stays at high effort above.

rules.when: subtle root-cause work that calls for read-only diagnosis first: an intermittent bug, a concurrency or race condition, an algorithmic problem, a security or data-integrity issue, highly coupled reasoning across a system, or a problem that has already survived repeated attempts, where the immediate deliverable is finding the root cause rather than fixing it yet (the scout form). This is a difficulty-of-reasoning test, not a size test - many files touched does not imply DEEP, and a single concurrency bug can. If the work is mostly settled, broad execution rather than an unsettled reasoning problem, that is IMPLEMENT-LARGE instead; if the deliverable is a forward structural recommendation rather than a diagnosis, that is ARCHITECTURE instead; if the deliverable is adversarial challenge of someone else's plan or claim rather than your own diagnosis, that is TENTH-MAN instead. If Opus 5.5's own diagnosis pass needs an independent alternative or escalation, that is the Sol-escalation rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Opus 5.5 at xhigh is the active, single-candidate primary for the read-only diagnosis form: find the root cause, do not fix it yet. This is not a quota-resolved peer of the Sol-escalation rule below - Opus 5.5 is the default diagnosis route, Sol is reached for only when that rule's escalation condition genuinely applies.

rules.when: the same read-only DEEP diagnosis work above, specifically when the Opus 5.5 diagnosis rule above is not enough and an independent alternative or escalation, on a different model family and harness, is genuinely needed. This is a separate, more specific rule within DEEP, not a routine default: pick it only when that escalation condition genuinely applies, never as a first choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-sol on Pi is the independent alternative/escalation for DEEP diagnosis, deliberately kept on a different harness and model family from the OMP Opus 5.5 primary above, preserving the existing Pi placement for this escalation in the diagnosis form. openai-codex/gpt-6-astra remains available only through the separate, more specific exceptional rule below, once even this Sol escalation leaves the diagnosis unresolved.

rules.when: the same reasoning-difficulty DEEP work above, once the difficult implementation and its supporting tools are clean enough to diagnose and fix in one session (the ship form), rather than requiring a separate read-only diagnosis pass first. If the Opus 5.5 ship pass leaves the problem unresolved, that is the Sol second-hypothesis rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Opus 5.5 at xhigh is the active, single-candidate primary once diagnosis and the difficult implementation belong in the same mutating session. This is not a quota-resolved peer of the Sol second-hypothesis rule below - Opus 5.5 runs first, Sol is reached for only after that rule's condition genuinely applies.

rules.when: the same mutating DEEP ship work above, specifically as a second hypothesis once the Opus 5.5 ship pass above has run and the problem remains unresolved. This is a separate, more specific rule within DEEP, not a routine default: pick it only after the Opus 5.5 pass has genuinely failed to resolve the problem, never as a first choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-sol on OMP is reached for only as a second hypothesis once the Opus 5.5 ship pass above leaves the problem unresolved, preserving the existing OMP placement for this escalation in the ship form. openai-codex/gpt-6-astra remains available only through the separate, more specific exceptional rule below, once even this Sol second hypothesis leaves the problem unresolved.

rules.when: the same reasoning-difficulty DEEP work above, in either the scout or ship form, specifically as the last escalation once the relevant Sol escalation above (scout diagnosis or ship second hypothesis) has already run and the problem remains genuinely unresolved. This is a separate, more specific rule within DEEP, not a routine default and not a quota-resolved peer of any rule above: pick it only after a Sol escalation has genuinely failed to resolve the problem, never as a first or second choice.
rules.why: openai-codex/gpt-6-astra on Pi is DEEP's last escalation, reached for only once the Opus 5.5 primary and the Sol escalation above have both failed to resolve the problem. Astra stays limited to this and this configuration's other genuinely exceptional lanes across both the scout and ship forms; it is never a routine DEEP default.

rules.when: frontend or browser-visible behavior: forms, validation, navigation, interactive components, browser-side state, or end-to-end user flows where automated tests can pass while real user behavior is wrong. If there is no browser-visible behavior at stake, that is IMPLEMENT instead. If the change is complex or cross-layer - delicate implementation, or frontend/backend changes that must stay consistent across layers - that is the complex-UI/BROWSER rule below instead.
rules.why: OMP + Sonnet at high effort, paired with this configuration's existing browser/manual verification policy (primary-policy.md section 7). Browser-visible surface alone is never a reason to reach for Opus or Astra as a default. If the underlying bug is a genuinely hard reasoning problem rather than an ordinary UI change, route it to DEEP instead and still apply browser verification to confirm the fix. Complex or cross-layer browser work is a separate, more specific rule below, not a quota-resolved peer of this ordinary case.

rules.when: the same browser-visible UI/BROWSER work above, specifically when the change is complex or cross-layer: delicate implementation (races, state machines, security-sensitive logic) or coordinated frontend/backend or multi-file changes that must stay consistent across layers, all of which must also be verified through the browser. This is a separate, more specific rule within UI/BROWSER, not a quota-resolved peer of the normal case: pick it only when that condition genuinely applies, not merely because a UI is involved.
rules.why: Opus 5.5 at high effort is reserved for complex or cross-layer UI/BROWSER work, still paired with this configuration's browser/manual verification policy (primary-policy.md section 7). Never a default for ordinary browser-visible changes.
